title: Fournier gangrene
subtitle: Necrotising infection of the perineum: cut early, cut again

sources.title: EAU Guidelines on Urological Infections: Fournier's gangrene (necrotising soft-tissue infection of the perineum)

sources.org: World Society of Emergency Surgery (WSES) and Surgical Infection Society Europe (SIS-E)
sources.title: 2018 WSES/SIS-E consensus conference: recommendations for the management of skin and soft-tissue infections (Sartelli M et al., World Journal of Emergency Surgery)
Surviving Sepsis Campaign: international guidelines for management of sepsis and septic shock 2021

red_flags.text: Perineal or scrotal pain out of proportion to what you can see. The skin is the last layer to show the disease.
Crepitus, dusky or black skin, blistering, or a thin grey foul-smelling discharge.
Systemic toxicity with a modest-looking perineal cellulitis, especially in a diabetic, an immunosuppressed or an alcohol-dependent patient.
Rapid spread of erythema or oedema across the perineum, penis, abdominal wall or thighs over hours.
A recent perianal abscess, urethral stricture, traumatic catheterisation or perineal procedure as the possible portal of entry.

do_now.text: Start empirical broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics covering Gram-positive, Gram-negative and anaerobic organisms on presentation, per local protocol, and refine them to culture results.
Book theatre for urgent radical debridement. Surgery is the treatment; antibiotics and resuscitation only buy time for it.
Resuscitate as septic shock: blood cultures, lactate, intravenous fluid, and early vasopressor support if hypotension persists.
Do not wait for imaging to confirm a clinical diagnosis in a toxic patient. Imaging must never delay debridement.

assess.text: Mark the edge of erythema with a pen and the time. Spread beyond the line within an hour or two is a decision in itself.
Examine the whole perineum, the anal canal, the penis and the abdominal wall. Look for the source: anorectal, urethral or skin.
A laboratory risk score can support suspicion of necrotising infection but has limited sensitivity. A low score never overrules a clinical diagnosis.
Glucose control and diabetic ketoacidosis screen; uncontrolled diabetes is the commonest predisposition.

investigate.text: Full blood count, renal function, electrolytes, glucose, C-reactive protein, lactate, coagulation, blood cultures, and group and save.
Tissue from the debridement for microscopy and culture. Superficial swabs are of little value.
CT pelvis and perineum in a stable patient when the diagnosis or the extent is genuinely uncertain, or to look for a retroperitoneal or pelvic source.

resuscitate.text: Intravenous fluid resuscitation and vasopressors to a target mean arterial pressure per sepsis guidance; critical care admission after the first debridement.
Correct glucose and electrolytes; start nutritional support early because the catabolic and wound losses are large.

definitive.text: Radical debridement of all necrotic skin, fascia and subcutaneous tissue back to bleeding, viable tissue. The testes usually have their own blood supply and are rarely involved.
Planned re-look in theatre within 24 to 48 hours, and repeat until no further necrosis is found.
Urinary diversion with a suprapubic catheter when the urethra is involved or the source is urethral; a urethral catheter otherwise keeps the wound dry.
Consider faecal diversion when the anal sphincter is involved or the wound cannot be kept clean.
Adjuncts such as hyperbaric oxygen have weak supporting evidence and must never delay or replace surgical debridement.
Reconstruction (delayed closure, grafts, flaps) only once the infection is controlled, with plastic surgery input.

escalate.text: Consultant urologist or general surgeon to theatre for the first debridement. This is not a first operation for an unsupervised trainee.
Critical care on the day of presentation.
Colorectal surgery for an anorectal source or sphincter involvement; plastic surgery for reconstruction; microbiology for antibiotic choice.

notes: Pain out of proportion and systemic toxicity with unimpressive skin is the classic presentation. If you are thinking about necrotising infection, the patient needs a surgeon to look at the fascia.
The first debridement is almost always too conservative. Plan the re-look before leaving theatre and tell the patient and family that more than one operation is expected.
Mortality is driven by delay to the first debridement. Time from the door to the knife is the metric that matters.
